[soft smile]  
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I work with new moms to see how you’re feeling emotionally in these first weeks and months after birth.  

I’m going to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand how you’re coping so we can offer the best support.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team, and we’ll take it at your pace. When we’re done, I’ll add up the score, explain what it means, and we’ll talk about any next steps or resources that might help.  

Ready to begin?  

1. In the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when life felt a little chaotic?

[slow breath, small shrug]  
Lately… I can still laugh, but it feels a little forced. Maybe a couple of times I actually giggled at something silly my husband said, but mostly I’m just too tired to find things funny. So, “not so often” would fit best.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slight shake of head]  
Definitely not as much as I used to. I’d say “not so often” fits—maybe once or twice when my husband made a joke, but even then it felt kind of flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[small sigh]  
Honestly… not very much. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week it’s like nothing sounds appealing. I still go through the motions, but the “looking-forward” part feels missing.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet voice, eyes on my lap]  
Yeah… sometimes. Like if the baby won’t settle, I’ll think, “Maybe I’m not doing something right,” or if the laundry piles up, I feel like I’m failing at the simplest stuff. It’s not constant, but it pops in a few times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[shifts in seat, fingers twisting the hem of my shirt]  
Yes… I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing, thinking, “What if she stops breathing when I put her down?” There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the pediatrician says so—but the worry just shows up, especially at night.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[small nod, voice a little shaky]  
A couple of times, mostly after dark—my chest gets tight, feels hard to breathe, like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. It passes if I rock the baby or step outside for a minute, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly]  
Yeah… most days. Between feedings, diapers, trying to squeeze in a nap that never really works, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I manage, but it’s that constant “behind” feeling—like I’m drowning in small stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet shrug]  
Not exactly “unhappy” keeping me awake—more like my mind won’t shut up about the next feeding or whether she’s breathing. I lie down and just stare at the ceiling for a while. Most nights this week it took me at least half an hour to drift off, even when the baby’s out.
I have felt sad or miserable

[small nod, eyes still on my lap]  
Yeah… I do feel that way some of the time. It’s not all day, but it hits in waves—like when I’m folding her tiny clothes or when the house is quiet. I’ll just get this heavy, sad feeling for a little while, then it lifts, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quick shake of head]  
No… I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt teary a couple of times, but the tears never come. It’s more that tight-throat, heavy-chest feeling than actual crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks up, eyes widen]  
No—never. I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just feel tired and overwhelmed, not like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary**

**Primary symptoms endorsed**  
- Marked reduction in ability to experience pleasure or laugh (Q1, Q2)  
- Frequent, unprovoked anxiety and nocturnal panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Daily self-blame/guilt over routine caregiving tasks (Q3)  
- Intermittent waves of sadness/misery without tearfulness (Q8)  
- Persistent sense of being overwhelmed/drowning in daily tasks (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia linked to intrusive worries about infant safety (Q7)  

**Patterns / risk indicators**  
- Consistent anhedonia and low mood congruent with depressive spectrum  
- prominent postpartum anxiety with nocturnal exacerbation  
- Negative cognitions focused on maternal competence  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood/anxiety, not infant schedule  
- Absence of self-harm ideation (Q10) – no acute safety concern noted  

**Screening observation**  
Responses indicate clinically significant mood and anxiety distress beginning post-delivery; constellation of anhedonia, excessive guilt, uncontrolled worry, sleep impairment, and impaired coping exceeds expected postpartum adjustment stress. Recommend follow-up with standardized diagnostic interview (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9/GAAD) and consideration of referral for perinatal mental-health evaluation.
